title: 128k Long-Context Runtime Performance Deep Dive - NovaHealth
summary: Deep technical session focused on supporting 128k+ token contexts for NovaHealth clinical search and summarization workflows. Discussed runtime bottlenecks, KV cache strategies, chunking/overlap trade-offs, quantization impact on perf/quality, and VPC/on-prem integration constraints. Agreed next steps: run 48h benchmark with sample dataset, share perf spreadsheet, and schedule an on-prem architecture review.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-08 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~78 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: Yes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE); Evan Chen (Redwood SE); Priya Rao (Redwood Solutions); Maya Ortiz (NovaHealth CTO); Dr. Alan Green (NovaHealth Head of ML); Lina Park (NovaHealth Infra); Tariq Hassan (NovaHealth Security)

Summary (auto): Deep dive on long-context (128k+) runtime perf, KV cache, batching, quantization, and VPC/on-prem constraints. Action items captured.

00:00 Samir Patel: Hey everyone thanks for joining, we did a quick agenda — start with constraints and workload, then show a couple perf numbers, KV cache approach, chunking heuristics, and then open Q&A.
01:02 Maya Ortiz: Thanks Samir, quick reminder our main driver is extracting and summarizing full longitudinal patient records and then doing multi-doc reasoning, so basically we need to feed 50k-200k tokens into the model sometimes. Latency target is sub-2s for short queries but for full summarization pipeline we can tolerate higher tail latencies if throughput is tight.
02:10 Evan Chen: Got it, that's helpful. Just to clarify, are you streaming partial summaries back to the UI or do you wait for full generation?
02:25 Maya Ortiz: We prefer streaming for UX but if the model takes a few minutes we chunk and then reassemble. Ideally streaming with progressive context would be great.
03:04 Dr. Alan Green: Also want to add quality bar — errors in hallucinated medfacts are a no-go; we need deterministic recall of references and patient identifiers masked.
03:45 Samir Patel: Totally — we'll call out where quantization or other optimizations can impact factuality. Evan, maybe start with a quick slide of the runtime trade-offs?
04:05 Evan Chen: Sure. High level: for 128k contexts the main bottlenecks are memory bandwidth for KV cache, attention computation (quadratic-ish if naive), and also tokenization/IO when pulling many docs. We use chunked attention patterns and prefix KV caching to avoid recomputing previous attention states where possible.
05:12 Evan Chen: (slide audio) So think of the runtime as three pieces — encode/ingest, KV cache management, and decode steps. With Redwood Dedicated you can pin GPU pools and we tune kernel selection based on sequence length distributions.
06:30 Lina Park: How does the KV cache scale when you have 200k tokens? Do you shard it across GPUs or spill to host memory?
06:55 Evan Chen: Good question. We typically do a hybrid: for the hot window (most recent ~64k tokens) we keep KV in GPU memory; for older prefixes we either compress (quantize keys/values) and keep them as 8-bit or spill to pinned host memory with fast NVMe-backed swap. For 128k we favor sharding across 2-4 GPUs depending on model size. There's some overhead on cross-GPU allgather for cache reads but we hide it with prefetching.
08:05 Lina Park: Prefetching to avoid stalls makes sense. Is there an API for controlling prefix retention?
08:18 Samir Patel: Yes, Redwood exposes retention policies: time-based, token-count-based, and landmark-based where you keep only summary vectors for very old prefixes. We can also expose a hook to evict by metadata e.g., patient-id.
09:02 Dr. Alan Green: On the chunking front, what's your recommended overlap size? We worry about missing cross-chunk references.
09:18 Evan Chen: Overlap is workload dependent. For clinical notes we see that 512-4096 tokens overlap often balances recall and compute. For longer docs we do smart chunking at sentence/section boundaries and add overlap plus an attention-windows trick — local attention inside chunks and sparse global tokens for cross-chunk heads.
10:00 Maya Ortiz: You mentioned attention optimizations — can you explain sliding vs global attention and the perf implications?
10:15 Evan Chen: Sliding window attention is O(n * w) where w is window size, so linear-ish versus quadratic. Global tokens are a sparse set of tokens that every chunk attends to — useful for doc-level anchors. The tradeoff: simpler sliding reduces compute but can miss long-range dependencies; adding a small number of global tokens recovers a lot of quality with modest perf cost.
11:20 Priya Rao: For 128k contexts we also recommend chunk-level embeddings + reranker — do a lightweight candidate retrieval with embeddings to limit what goes into the full autoregressive pass. That reduces end-to-end cost a lot.
12:05 Lina Park: Okay that helps. On quantization — we saw claims that 4-bit can save cost but may degrade quality. What's your experience?
12:20 Evan Chen: Right — 4-bit quantization (GPTQ-style) yields large memory and perf wins but is model-dependent. For many LLaMA-style weights 4-bit with some outlier handling is acceptable for retrieval/summarization tasks but for clinical QA we often recommend 8-bit or mixed precision for critical inference to avoid subtle degradation. We can run head-to-head evals on your prompts.
13:30 Dr. Alan Green: Any automated quality regression detection when you change quantization?
13:40 Samir Patel: Yes — Redwood Optimize includes eval hooks tied to prompt sets. We can run regression tests across candidate quantized variants and raise alerts if key metrics drop. We'll include that in the bench plan.
14:10 Maya Ortiz: Let's talk numbers — what latency/throughput should we expect for a 128k end-to-end summation?
14:25 Evan Chen: It depends a lot on model size and how much you prefilter. Ballpark: with a 13B-ish model optimized and sharded across 2 A100/4090-ish GPUs you might see end-to-end 30-90 seconds for a full 128k generation if doing full autoregressive. With heavy chunking + rerank + partial streaming you can cut that to 6-20s for user-facing summaries. Dedicated multi-GPU rigs or Atlas instances reduce the variance.
16:05 Lina Park: Are these numbers from internal benchmarks or public? We need reproducible configs.
16:15 Evan Chen: Internal; we will provide the exact config, kernel flags, batch sizes and quantization steps in the perf spreadsheet.
17:00 Tariq Hassan: Security question: if we move older KV to host/NVMe how is data encrypted at rest and how do we integrate with our KMS?
17:12 Samir Patel: We support customer-managed KMS for private deployments; NVMe-backed swap is encrypted with the same keys and we provide audit logs for evictions/reads. For Hosted we have strict tenant separation and SOC2 controls. We'll share the KMS integration guide.
18:20 Maya Ortiz: For on-prem we will need RBAC and SSO.
18:30 Samir Patel: Redwood Private supports SAML SSO, RBAC, and audit trails. We can scope the enterprise package in the next step.
19:05 Evan Chen: Back to perf — batching is another lever. For latency-sensitive single queries, you run small batch sizes to keep tail low. For throughput (e.g., nightly summarization), you can pack many documents and gain GPU utilization. We have adaptive batching: route low-latency traffic to an isolated pool and run large batch jobs in a background pool.
20:12 Dr. Alan Green: Can we do hybrid — streaming partial results while batch continues?
20:25 Evan Chen: Yes, we often stream top-k token prefixes while background jobs fill in deeper context. There's complexity in merging and consistency but it's doable.
21:10 Maya Ortiz: How about model fallbacks if GPU capacity is constrained?
21:20 Samir Patel: Redwood routing supports policy-based fallbacks to smaller quantized variants or CPU fallback for non-critical tasks. For critical clinical inference we recommend pre-reserved Dedicated capacity.
22:03 Priya Rao: Quick demo note — I have a short perf trace showing KV cache hit rates with and without compression, would you like me to share?
22:20 Maya Ortiz: Yes please that would help.
23:00 Priya Rao: (screen share) This trace shows a 70% hit-rate for live sessions with prefix retention; when we spill to host and compress we drop to 62% but save ~40% memory.
24:25 Lina Park: Do you have recommended thresholds for evicting by patient-id? We want to keep active patients hot.
24:40 Evan Chen: We recommend a hot set policy: keep any patient with activity in the last 24h pinned in GPU memory; evict older ones to compressed host memory and keep summary embeddings for quick retrieval.
26:05 Dr. Alan Green: On chunking heuristics, how do you keep citations aligned when you recombine chunks?
26:20 Evan Chen: We store provenance metadata per chunk (source doc, token ranges) and when we do answer synthesis we emit citations by mapping tokens back to original chunks. There's an accuracy tradeoff if you use heavy summarization, so we keep the citation step separate and deterministic.
27:40 Maya Ortiz: Let's talk cost — how much extra are we paying for Dedicated with multi-GPU and NVMe?
27:55 Samir Patel: Pricing depends on commit and instance type. We'll send a detailed cost sheet but expect Dedicated to be multiplex host API rates — but you get predictable throughput and support SLAs. We'll include pricing scenarios for pilot and scale.
29:10 Lina Park: We want to run a 48h bench. What should we include?
29:20 Evan Chen: Include representative queries, batch vs single-entry patterns, a sample corpus up to 200k tokens per session, and metrics: wall time, p50/p95/p99, token throughput, KV hit rates, memory usage, and quality metrics (exact match, rouge for summaries). Also record model variants and quantization.
31:00 Maya Ortiz: Sounds good. A few detailed questions from my team — what about attention optimization libraries and custom kernels?
31:20 Evan Chen: We use a kernel selector at runtime; for different sequence lengths we pick different CUDA kernels and memory layouts. For very long contexts we enable fused attention kernels and memory-efficient attention (e.g., flash attention variants) when supported by the hardware. We also have a fallback slower path for hardware without those ops.
32:50 Priya Rao: Note: some of these optimizations require specific CUDA/CUDNN/driver versions; we'll include compatibility matrix.
33:30 Tariq Hassan: For on-prem, can we bring our own HSM for keys?
33:40 Samir Patel: Yes, Redwood Private supports HSM integration; we can exchange integration docs.
34:25 Dr. Alan Green: Any quick wins we can try before the full bench?
34:40 Evan Chen: Yes: 1) implement a retrieval filter to cut context to 30-50k before expensive generation; 2) try 8-bit quantization first; 3) tune chunk overlap to 1k tokens and validate quality.
36:05 Maya Ortiz: Good. On streaming, how do you handle partial hallucinations or inconsistencies mid-stream?
36:20 Evan Chen: We add a verification step where the streaming tokens are soft-committed and then a short certifier reruns critical spans for factual checks using a smaller verifier model. It adds latency but improves safety.
37:40 Lina Park: For the 48h bench we'll want logs/metrics exported to our Prometheus/Grafana. Is that supported?
37:55 Samir Patel: Yes, Redwood exposes metrics endpoints and we can pump logs to your SIEM or Prometheus. We'll share the exporter config.
38:30 Priya Rao: Quick note on chunk embeddings — if you precompute embeddings you can avoid re-encoding stable docs and save lots of compute.
39:00 Dr. Alan Green: For the bench, what GPU types do you recommend we test on-prem?
39:10 Evan Chen: Test on A100 40GB, 80GB if you have, and also newer Ada-generation if available. For cost-sensitivity also test on 4090/4080-class cards with good NVMe backing. We'll give exact instance specs.
40:25 Maya Ortiz: A question about compliance — you said audit logs for reads from NVMe; can we tie them to patient access requests?
40:35 Tariq Hassan: (adds) We need per-read auditability for any patient data touches.
40:45 Samir Patel: Yes we can map reads to request IDs and surface them in the audit trail. We'll include that in the security doc.
41:20 Evan Chen: Another perf knob is packing multiple conversations into single forward passes when the model supports multi-batch sequences; good for throughput but bad for tail latency.
42:00 Priya Rao: Example: if you have 100 short summaries, pack them into a batch and you get much better GPU utilization.
42:40 Lina Park: For our use-case we will have intermittent spikes; what's the burst capacity approach?
42:50 Samir Patel: For Dedicated we offer burst pools and autoscaling policies with warm standby nodes; for on-prem we can design spare capacity or allow overflow to Hosted with encrypted transit.
43:30 Maya Ortiz: Overflow to Hosted is interesting but we have residency constraints.
43:40 Samir Patel: We can do region pinning and hybrid routing to respect residency. For regulated data we recommend Private.
44:10 Dr. Alan Green: A practical question: how do we validate that chunking doesn't break entities across splits?
44:25 Evan Chen: Use overlap heuristics and entity-aware splitters; also run unit tests on a labeled subset to check entity continuity. We'll help set that up.
45:00 Priya Rao: I'll share a notebook that runs chunking experiments and visualizes token boundaries.
45:20 Lina Park: On the NVMe compression: what compression ratio and CPU overhead should we expect?
45:30 Evan Chen: With fast lightweight compressors we see ~2-3x compression with moderate CPU cost; more aggressive compression saves more space but adds latency. We tune for your throughput profile.
46:10 Maya Ortiz: If we go to 4-bit quantization will that break our citation mapping?
46:20 Evan Chen: Quantization affects weights, not token->source mapping. Citation mapping is a metadata layer so it's independent; quality changes could change selection but mapping remains intact.
47:05 Dr. Alan Green: For the bench, please include a few clinical-critical prompts to check hallucination rates.
47:15 Samir Patel: Will do.
48:00 Priya Rao: Quick note: we also support prioritized KV read — hot keys get faster path.
48:30 Lina Park: That could be useful for high-priority patients.
49:00 Evan Chen: Regarding attention -- for some models we can do asymmetric attention: large global heads and small local heads to keep compute down while preserving long-range signals.
50:10 Maya Ortiz: Do you have any reference docs on the kernel selector and attention settings?
50:20 Priya Rao: We'll send the runtime tuning guide and kernel compatibility matrix.
51:00 Tariq Hassan: For on-prem, network egress is a concern. If we do hybrid with Hosted for bursts, what about encryption in flight?
51:12 Samir Patel: TLS everywhere, and we can do mutual TLS and private network peering for lower attack surface.
52:00 Dr. Alan Green: If we pin models and release rollouts, how do we rollback if a quantized variant regresses?
52:12 Evan Chen: Rollbacks are supported via model versioning and canary routes; Redwood Console can auto-failover to previous variant if quality metrics drop.
53:00 Maya Ortiz: Great. Let's confirm the bench timeline and who's owning which artifacts.
53:12 Samir Patel: Action items captured — Evan will run the bench, Samir will send pricing and docs, Lina will provide corpus, Tariq will provide security questions.
54:00 Priya Rao: I'll prepare the on-prem proposal and a notebook for chunking.
55:00 Maya Ortiz: Anything else from the team?
55:10 Dr. Alan Green: Could we run an initial micro-bench with a 32k slice to validate configs faster?
55:20 Evan Chen: Absolutely, we can do a 32k pilot within 48 hours and then scale to full 128k.
56:00 Lina Park: We'll aim to share corpus by 2026-07-09.
56:12 Samir Patel: Perfect. We'll follow up with the perf spreadsheet and a calendar invite for the on-prem architecture review.
57:00 Maya Ortiz: Thanks everyone.
57:05 Samir Patel: Thanks — talk soon.

(Recording ends)
